title: Factoring sparse polynomials
subject: algorithms
summary: Sparse polynomials are encoded by their nonzero terms. Large exponents and dense factors make this a different algorithmic problem from dense factorization.
field: number fields and general coefficient fields
questionsAnswered: Why can sparse input have a factor too large to print efficiently?
How are factors of bounded degree found?
What improves when each variable has bounded degree?

sections.title: Input and output
sections.body:
A sparse polynomial is stored by listing its nonzero coefficients and exponent vectors. Exponents may be written in binary. Thus \(x^N-1\) has input length of order \(\log N\), apart from coefficient encoding. When \(N=\ell\) is prime, its factor \(\Phi_\ell(x)=1+x+\cdots+x^{\ell-1}\) has \(\ell\) terms. An algorithm that prints every factor densely cannot always run in time polynomial in sparse input length.

In several variables, individual degree at most \(d\) means \(\deg_{x_i}f\le d\) for every variable. This differs from allowing one variable an arbitrarily large binary exponent.

sections.title: Factors of bounded degree
sections.body:
Lenstra gives a deterministic algorithm which, for a number field \(K\), a nonzero sparse \(f\in K[x]\), and \(d\ge1\), finds all monic irreducible factors of degree at most \(d\), with multiplicities. Its running time is polynomial in the encoded lengths of \(K,f\) and in \(d\), not in \(\log d\).

Cyclotomic factors are treated separately. For other factors, a lower bound for the height of a root shows that a sufficiently large gap splits a vanishing sum into two vanishing blocks. Factoring shorter blocks then finds the required factors.

sections.title: Complexity of irreducibility
sections.body:
For univariate integer polynomials with binary exponents, a 2026 preprint of Cao–Gao–Huang–Nie claims that irreducibility is coNP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions. Their construction gives monic polynomials. Equivalently, reducibility is NP-hard under these reductions. The title’s NP-hardness assertion for irreducibility uses a different notion: a polynomial-time Turing reduction with one oracle query.

The preprint also claims membership in \(\mathsf{PP}\subseteq\mathsf{PSPACE}\). Here \(\mathsf{PP}\) allows an arbitrarily small advantage over probability \(1/2\); it does not give a bounded-error randomized polynomial-time algorithm. The upper bound assumes a fixed positive zero-free gap for Dedekind zeta functions of all number fields, together with a uniform effective prime-ideal estimate. The authors invoke recent preprints for these analytic inputs; Appendix A.4–A.5 retains them as hypotheses of the formalized theorem. Both complexity results are recorded as unpublished claims. They concern unbounded binary exponents, so they do not settle the bounded-individual-degree question below.

citations.locator: Version 1, Theorems 4 and 10; Remark 3; §3.1; Appendix A.4–A.5

sections.title: How many terms can a factor have?
sections.body:
Let \(0\ne f\in F[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), where \(F\) is a field, have at most \(s\) terms and individual degree at most \(d\). Then Bhargava–Saraf–Volkovich prove that every factor has at most \(s^{O(d^2\log(n+1))}\) terms. Their proof uses Newton polytopes. It yields deterministic quasipolynomial factorization when \(d\) is fixed.

This bounds the number of terms in factors, not just their degrees. The cost of univariate factorization over the coefficient field must also be included.

citations.locator: Theorems 1 and 2 of the arXiv manuscript
citations.note: The equivalent log(n+1) bound avoids a convention at n=1; add a dummy variable to treat that case.

sections.title: Sparse divisors
sections.body:
Chuyoon–Shpilka’s CCC 2026 paper lists all \(s\)-sparse divisors not divisible by a nonconstant monomial in time \(\operatorname{poly}(n,d!,s^d)\), up to nonzero scalar multiples. It also gives full factorization in time \(\operatorname{poly}(n,s^{d^2\log(n+1)})\). These bounds suppress univariate-factorization and field-arithmetic costs.

Finding sparse divisors does not settle irreducibility: a proper factor may have more terms than the input.

citations.locator: Theorems 9 and 12; Remark 7, published CCC 2026 version
citations.note: The input is the nonzero polynomial defined above; log(n+1) gives a bound valid also for n=1.

sections.title: Lists of candidate factors
sections.body:
The June 2026 preprint of Bhattacharjee–Kothary–Rai–Saraf gives a different output. In characteristic zero or greater than \(d\), it constructs at most \(s^d\) constant-depth circuits containing every factor not divisible by a nonconstant monomial, up to scalar multiples, in time \(\operatorname{poly}(n,d!,s^d)\). The maximal monomial divisor is returned separately.

Some circuits may represent polynomials which do not divide \(f\). Small coefficient fields may require an extension, and univariate-factorization costs are suppressed. Thus the list alone is not a factorization certificate. Interpolation and divisibility tests give complete factorization with the known quasipolynomial bound.

related.why: The input representation and output size affect complexity.
Large exponent gaps separate factors with roots of positive height.

questions.title: Can bounded individual degree give a faster irreducibility test?
questions.scope: An n-variable, s-sparse polynomial of individual degree at most d; field costs stated separately
questions.body: Chuyoon–Shpilka ask for a deterministic irreducibility test in time \(\operatorname{poly}(n,s^d)\). Their full manuscript states this question in §10; the published conference paper gives the sparse-divisor and full-factorization algorithms discussed above. A proper factor may be denser than the input, and a list of circuits containing all factors can also contain polynomials that do not divide the input.

title: Ehrhart polynomials
subject: families
summary: Ehrhart polynomials count lattice points in dilated polytopes. Their factors and Galois groups connect polyhedral geometry with arithmetic.
status: Published computations and a cited open question
questionsAnswered: What is the Ehrhart polynomial of a lattice polytope?
How do simple polytopes give different Galois groups?

sections.title: Definition and example
sections.body:
For a lattice polytope \(P\subset\mathbb R^m\), the function \(L_P(t)=|tP\cap\mathbb Z^m|\), for integers \(t\ge0\), is a polynomial in \(\mathbb Q[t]\) of degree \(\dim P\). Its constant term is \(1\).

For \(P=[-1,1]^m\), coordinate counting gives \(L_P(t)=(2t+1)^m\). Its splitting field is \(\mathbb Q\), and its Galois group is trivial. Ehrhart polynomials need not be irreducible or squarefree.

sections.title: Example
sections.body:
For the standard simplex \(\operatorname{conv}(0,e_1,\ldots,e_d)\), lattice points in its \(t\)-th dilate are nonnegative integer vectors with sum at most \(t\). Counting them gives

\[L_P(t)=\binom{t+d}{d}=\frac{(t+1)\cdots(t+d)}{d!}.\]

Thus the polynomial splits over \(\mathbb Q\). This follows directly from the lattice-point count.

For the different simplex \(S=\operatorname{conv}(e_1,\ldots,e_d,-e_1-\cdots-e_d)\), Fieker–Hofmann–Joswig give

\[L_S(t)=\binom{t+d+1}{d+1}-\binom{t}{d+1}.\]

In dimension two this is \((3t^2+3t+2)/2\), with discriminant \(-15/4\). Its group is \(C_2\). Their Theorem 4 describes the group for this family in every dimension.

sections.title: Computing the group
sections.body: Fieker–Hofmann–Joswig apply subgroup descent in OSCAR to Ehrhart polynomials. They combine permutation groups, relative invariants, and certified root approximations. Their software comparisons concern the 2022 versions.

related.why: Subgroup descent determines the root permutation group.
The defining polynomial must arise from lattice-point counting.

questions.title: Which finite groups occur for Ehrhart polynomials?
questions.scope: Splitting fields of Ehrhart polynomials of arbitrary lattice polytopes over Q
questions.body: Question 6 asks which groups occur, and specifically whether every finite cyclic group occurs. No irreducibility assumption is imposed. The question restricts inverse Galois theory to polynomials arising from lattice-point counts.

citations.locator: §4, Question 6, p. 7 of the published version
